chapter: Early Los Angeles and first bands
title: Charlie Echols, the West Coast Cab Calloway
summary: He describes Charlie Echols, a bandleader who could not play but fronted good musicians like Cab Calloway.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: All right, so after the Arabee, it seems the band broke up and like you mentioned, Charlie Echols. Charlie Echols was the west coast's Cab Calloway. Charles Echols. He used to get a lot of gigs -- but he always wanted the best musicians. He could not play a note, but he stood in front of the band like Cab and he would sing these songs and he would conduct the band and shake his head because he imitated Cab, really, but not -- he couldn't scat and all that, but I mean he was the west coast's Cab Calloway, and he was good for a lot of the musicians because he was a personality, and he got a lot of jobs for them and he had a lot of good musicians working in the band, you know.

I played with him much later, but you know, at this point in time, I didn't work with him yet, but it seems to me after Buck Clayton, I really started getting my recognition, you know, at Stuff Smith came out ... I know this is in '37-- Stuff Smith came out, oh, let's see ... no, I got to go back.
